subject: biochemistry
title: Carbohydrate synthesis and storage: gluconeogenesis, glycogen metabolism and storage diseases

steps.tx: Gluconeogenesis synthesizes glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors, primarily lactate, glycerol, and **glucogenic** amino acids during fasting. Because three glycolytic reactions are irreversible, gluconeogenesis employs four bypass enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase bypass pyruvate kinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase bypasses phosphofructokinase-1, and glucose-6-phosphatase hydrolyzes glucose-6-phosphate to release free glucose into the systemic circulation.
steps.say: Gluconeogenesis generates glucose from lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids during fasting. Four bypass enzymes overcome irreversible glycolytic steps: pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and hepatic glucose-6-phosphatase.

rows: Present in liver and renal cortex, absent in muscle

steps.tx: The bifunctional **enzyme** PFK-2/FBPase-2 regulates reciprocal flux between glycolysis and gluconeogenesis via fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. Glucagon phosphorylates the enzyme via protein kinase A, activating the phosphatase domain and degrading fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. Relieved of allosteric inhibition, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase stimulates gluconeogenesis. Insulin promotes dephosphorylation, activating the kinase domain, elevating fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, and strongly stimulating phosphofructokinase-1.
steps.say: The bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2 controls glycolysis and gluconeogenesis via fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. Glucagon phosphorylates the enzyme, activating phosphatase activity to degrade fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and drive gluconeogenesis. Insulin dephosphorylates the enzyme to activate kinase activity and promote glycolysis.

left.title: Fasted state (Glucagon dominance)
points: Elevated cyclic AMP and active protein kinase A

steps.tx: Glycogen synthesis and degradation are coordinated by reciprocal **phosphorylation** cascades. Glycogen synthase elongates alpha-1,4 chains using UDP-glucose, active when dephosphorylated by insulin-stimulated phosphatase. Glycogen phosphorylase cleaves terminal residues to glucose-1-phosphate, activated when phosphorylated by phosphorylase kinase. Debranching enzyme transfers three residues and cleaves the alpha-1,6 branch point, releasing one free glucose molecule per branch point.
steps.say: Glycogen synthesis and breakdown depend on opposing phosphorylation states. Glycogen synthase elongates chains using UDP-glucose, activated when dephosphorylated by insulin. Glycogen phosphorylase cleaves glucose-1-phosphate, activated by phosphorylation. Debranching enzyme removes alpha-1,6 branch points.

steps.tx: Inborn errors of glycogen metabolism manifest as distinct **storage** diseases. Type I (von Gierke disease) arises from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, causing severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, and hyperuricemia. Type II (Pompe disease) is a lysosomal acid maltase deficiency causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Type V (McArdle disease) impairs skeletal muscle phosphorylase, producing exercise-induced painful cramping, myoglobinuria, and absent post-exercise venous lactate elevation.
steps.say: Glycogen storage diseases result from specific enzyme mutations. Von Gierke disease impairs glucose-6-phosphatase, causing severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly. Pompe disease impairs lysosomal acid maltase, causing fatal cardiomyopathy. McArdle disease lacks muscle phosphorylase, causing exercise cramps and myoglobinuria.

rows: Hepatomegaly, normal blood lactate, limit dextrins
